seo.title: 45 Best Jewelry Logos Explained by a Brand Designer [2026]
seo.description: 45 jewelry brand logos with names, explained by a brand designer: luxury houses like Cartier, Tiffany & Co., and Bulgari, designer labels, accessible brands, and jewelry retailers.

description: 45 jewelry brand logos with names, explained by a brand designer: luxury houses like Cartier, Tiffany & Co., and Bulgari, designer labels, accessible brands, and jewelry retailers.
intro:
A jewelry logo has to work on a tiny clasp, a ring box, a shopping bag, and a store front, and it has to feel as precious as the pieces it sells. The best jewelry logos are simple, refined, and built from carefully chosen type, often with a single detail that signals craft or heritage.

What makes a good jewelry logo?

Typography that feels precious: most jewelry brands use a wordmark, from the flowing script of Cartier to the Roman capitals of Bulgari. The letterforms carry the luxury.

One detail of craft or heritage: the best logos add one small idea, like the Roman V in Bulgari, the crown on the Pandora O, or the diamond-cut A in Zales.

Restraint in colour: jewelry logos are usually black, gold, or one signature tone, so the packaging and the stones do the talking, like Tiffany Blue or the Cartier red box.

Below are 45 jewelry brand logos with names, in five groups: iconic jewelry houses, heritage fine jewelers, designer fine jewelry, accessible and demi-fine brands, and jewelry retailers. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. If you are building a premium jewelry brand, see how I approach luxury branding, and read my guides to fashion logos, monogram logos, and logo fonts.

logoResearch.name: Cartier
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Louis-François Cartier founded the house in Paris in 1847.
observations: The flowing script looks like a signature, which makes the brand feel personal and handcrafted.
The large, curled C gives the wordmark a strong first letter that works almost like a monogram.

logoResearch.name: Tiffany & Co.
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Charles Lewis Tiffany and John B. Young founded Tiffany & Co. in New York in 1837, and LVMH has owned it since 2021.
observations: Classic serif capitals keep the wordmark formal and timeless.
The logo stays black so that Tiffany Blue, the brand's famous colour, can live on the boxes and bags.

logoResearch.name: Bulgari
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sotirio Bulgari opened his first shop in Rome in 1884.
observations: The wordmark uses a V instead of a U, like the letters carved into ancient Roman monuments.
Very wide spacing gives the short name a monumental, classical feel.

logoResearch.name: Van Cleef & Arpels
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Van Cleef & Arpels opened on Place Vendôme in Paris in 1906, after the marriage of Alfred Van Cleef and Estelle Arpels.
observations: Light, elegant serif type keeps the long name graceful.
The ampersand joins the two family names, which tells the brand's origin story.

logoResearch.name: Harry Winston
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Harry Winston founded his company in New York in 1932 and became known as the "King of Diamonds".
observations: Spaced serif capitals give the founder's name a quiet, confident feel.
The logo stays simple so the diamonds, not the brand mark, are the stars.

logoResearch.name: Graff
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Laurence Graff founded Graff in London in 1960.
observations: Extremely wide spacing makes a five-letter name feel grand and expensive.
The thin capitals are almost architectural, like letters on a Bond Street shop front.

logoResearch.name: Chopard
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Louis-Ulysse Chopard founded the company in Sonvilier, Switzerland, in 1860, and the Scheufele family has owned it since 1963.
observations: The calligraphic script gives the watch and jewelry house a personal, handwritten feel.
The small "Genève" line underneath ties the brand to Swiss watchmaking.

logoResearch.name: Boucheron
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Frédéric Boucheron opened his first boutique in Paris in 1858 and was the first modern jeweller on Place Vendôme in 1893.
observations: Heavy serif capitals make the name feel solid and established.
"Paris depuis 1858" underneath turns the founding date into part of the logo.

logoResearch.name: Chaumet
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chaumet traces its roots to 1780 in Paris, and its founder Marie-Étienne Nitot was jeweller to Napoleon.
observations: The ornamental emblem above the name recalls a tiara, the jewel Chaumet is most famous for.
Classic serif capitals and a small "Paris" line keep the logo regal.

logoResearch.name: Piaget
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Georges Piaget founded the company in La Côte-aux-Fées, Switzerland, in 1874 as a watch movement workshop.
observations: Tall, condensed serif capitals make the name feel elegant and slim, like a thin watch.
The logo has no symbol, so the distinctive letter shapes carry the brand.

logoResearch.name: Buccellati
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mario Buccellati opened his shop in Milan in 1919, and the brand is known for its engraved, textured gold.
observations: The ornamental emblem above the name looks like Buccellati's hand-engraved metalwork.
Thin capitals and "Milano dal 1919" keep the logo light and refined.

logoResearch.name: De Beers
logoResearch.verifiedFact: De Beers was founded in 1888, and its slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" dates from 1947.
observations: Small-caps serif letters give the name a traditional, trustworthy feel.
The famous slogan sits under the name, so the logo carries the brand's best-known idea.

logoResearch.name: Mikimoto
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kokichi Mikimoto created the first cultured pearl in 1893 and opened his Ginza store in Tokyo in 1899.
observations: Wide serif capitals make the name calm and balanced, like a string of pearls.
The plain wordmark lets the pearls, the brand's signature, speak for themselves.

logoResearch.name: Damiani
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Enrico Grassi Damiani founded the brand in Valenza, Italy, in 1924.
observations: Heavy, high-contrast serif capitals give the name strength and presence.
The small line "Handmade in Italy since 1924" adds craft and heritage.

logoResearch.name: Pomellato
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pino Rabolini founded Pomellato in Milan in 1967, and Kering has owned it since 2013.
observations: The loose, hand-drawn script feels playful and artistic, unlike most fine jewelers.
The big looped P gives the logo a memorable first letter.

logoResearch.name: Fred
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Fred Samuel opened his first jewelry shop in Paris in 1936, and the brand has been part of LVMH since 1995.
observations: Flared serif capitals give the short name a classic Parisian feel.
The long tail of the R sweeps under the letters like a wave, giving a simple wordmark one memorable detail.

logoResearch.name: Garrard
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Garrard was founded in London in 1735 and served as the British Crown Jeweller from 1843 to 2007.
observations: Strong serif capitals make the name feel official and established.
"London 1735" underneath tells the brand's royal heritage in two words.

logoResearch.name: Asprey
logoResearch.verifiedFact: William Asprey founded the company in Mitcham, Surrey, in 1781, and its flagship is on London's New Bond Street.
observations: An elegant lowercase serif makes the name feel refined and English.
The signature Asprey purple sets the logo apart from black-only rivals.

logoResearch.name: David Yurman
logoResearch.verifiedFact: David and Sybil Yurman founded the company in New York in 1980, and its cable bracelet is the signature piece.
observations: Wide, geometric capitals make the founder's name modern and architectural.
The generous spacing gives the logo a calm, premium feel.

logoResearch.name: Messika
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Valérie Messika founded the brand in Paris in 2005.
observations: Bold geometric capitals make the young brand feel modern and confident.
The small "Paris" line underneath links it to the city of high jewelry.

logoResearch.name: Repossi
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Repossi was founded in Turin in 1920 and is now led by fourth-generation designer Gaia Repossi.
observations: Widely spaced serif capitals look like a classic Italian jeweller's sign.
The tiny Place Vendôme address underneath shows where the brand lives today.

logoResearch.name: Jessica McCormack
logoResearch.verifiedFact: New Zealand-born designer Jessica McCormack runs her brand from a townhouse in London's Mayfair.
observations: Spaced serif capitals give the name a classic, Georgian feel.
The raised small c in "Mc" is a traditional typographic detail that adds charm.

logoResearch.name: Sophie Buhai
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sophie Buhai launched her jewelry label in Los Angeles in 2014.
observations: Condensed, bold capitals give the name a strong, graphic look.
The tall letters feel modern and sculptural, like the brand's pieces.

logoResearch.name: Anita Ko
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Anita Ko launched her fine jewelry line in Los Angeles in 2006.
observations: Thin, wide geometric capitals keep the short name light and modern.
The minimal logo suits a brand known for clean, modern fine jewelry.

logoResearch.name: Suzanne Kalan
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Suzanne Kalan's Los Angeles brand is known for its baguette-cut stones.
observations: Bold, spaced capitals make the founder's name strong and modern.
The geometric letters echo the clean lines of baguette-cut gems.

logoResearch.name: Spinelli Kilcollin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Yves Spinelli and Dylan Kilcollin founded the brand in Los Angeles in 2010, and it is known for linked rings.
observations: A classic serif joins the two founders' names in one line.
The traditional type balances the brand's modern, architectural ring designs.

logoResearch.name: Jennifer Meyer
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jennifer Meyer launched her fine jewelry line in Los Angeles in 2005.
observations: Very wide spacing turns the founder's name into a light, airy wordmark.
Thin capitals match the brand's delicate, everyday pieces.

logoResearch.name: Pandora
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Per and Winnie Enevoldsen founded Pandora as a jewelry shop in Copenhagen in 1982.
observations: The small crown above the O makes the bold wordmark feel precious.
Heavy, rounded capitals make the brand feel friendly and accessible.

logoResearch.name: Swarovski
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Daniel Swarovski founded the company in Wattens, Austria, in 1895 to cut crystal.
observations: Condensed, high-contrast capitals make the name sharp and glamorous.
The thin and thick strokes echo the facets of cut crystal.

logoResearch.name: Mejuri
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Noura Sakkijha founded Mejuri in Toronto in 2015 as an online fine jewelry brand.
observations: Heavy, tightly spaced capitals make the logo bold and digital-first.
The strong wordmark works as well on Instagram as on packaging.

logoResearch.name: Alex and Ani
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Carolyn Rafaelian founded Alex and Ani in Rhode Island in 2004, naming it after her daughters.
observations: Thin, wide capitals keep the long name light and approachable.
Spelling out "and" instead of an ampersand makes the logo feel friendly and personal.

logoResearch.name: Monica Vinader
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Monica Vinader founded her jewelry brand in London in 2008.
observations: Wide, evenly spaced capitals make the founder's name clean and modern.
The geometric letters suit the brand's simple, stackable designs.

logoResearch.name: Missoma
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Marisa Hordern founded Missoma in London in 2007.
observations: Geometric capitals with a perfectly round O make the logo modern and balanced.
The clean wordmark works across a digital-first, fashion-led brand.

logoResearch.name: Thomas Sabo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Thomas Sabo founded his jewelry company in Germany in 1984.
observations: The logo is a handwritten signature, which makes the brand feel personal.
The quick, slanted strokes suit a brand built on charms and personal style.

logoResearch.name: Astrid & Miyu
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Connie Nam founded Astrid & Miyu in London in 2012.
observations: Wide, thin capitals make the name feel light and modern.
The ampersand in the middle balances the two invented names.

logoResearch.name: Catbird
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Catbird started as a small shop in Brooklyn, New York, in 2004.
observations: The hand-lettered script feels personal and a little quirky, like the shop itself.
"Est. 2004" underneath gives the young brand a sense of history.

logoResearch.name: Chow Tai Fook
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chow Tai Fook was founded in Guangzhou in 1929 and is now one of the world's largest jewelry retailers.
observations: Bold Chinese characters on a red block make the logo instantly recognizable in Asia.
Red is the colour of luck in Chinese culture, which suits a jewelry brand.

logoResearch.name: Tanishq
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tanishq was launched in 1994 by Titan, part of India's Tata Group.
observations: Custom lettering with curved strokes gives the name an Indian, handcrafted feel.
The T monogram above the name works on its own on boxes and stores.

logoResearch.name: Blue Nile
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Blue Nile was founded in Seattle in 1999 as an online diamond retailer.
observations: A bold serif in navy blue makes the online brand feel established and trustworthy.
The name itself suggests the colour, which the logo uses directly.

logoResearch.name: Brilliant Earth
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Beth Gerstein and Eric Grossberg founded Brilliant Earth in San Francisco in 2005, focusing on ethically sourced jewelry.
observations: Thin, widely spaced capitals feel light and modern.
The name signals the brand's ethical sourcing mission before you read anything else.

logoResearch.name: Zales
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Morris and William Zale founded Zales in Wichita Falls, Texas, in 1924.
observations: Wide capitals in deep purple make the name stand out in shopping malls.
The A is drawn like a cut diamond, a simple idea that ties the logo to the product.

logoResearch.name: Kay Jewelers
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kay Jewelers was founded in Reading, Pennsylvania, in 1916 and is now part of Signet Jewelers.
observations: Heavy, wide capitals make the three-letter name easy to read from across a mall.
The short name works like a friendly nickname, which suits a mainstream jeweller.

logoResearch.name: Helzberg Diamonds
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Morris Helzberg founded the company in Kansas City, Kansas, in 1915, and Berkshire Hathaway has owned it since 1995.
observations: Classic serif capitals give the family name a traditional feel.
"1915" underneath stresses more than a century of heritage.

logoResearch.name: Mappin & Webb
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mappin & Webb traces its roots to Sheffield in 1775 and holds a Royal Warrant as a silversmith.
observations: A light, spaced serif keeps the long name elegant.
The ampersand joins the two family names, like many heritage British firms.

logoResearch.name: Tous
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tous started as a watch repair shop in Manresa, Spain, in 1920, and its teddy bear became the brand's symbol in 1985.
observations: Heavy, compact capitals make the four-letter name bold and playful.
The strong wordmark balances the cute teddy bear used on the jewelry itself.

listIntro: The boards below show all 45 jewelry logos in one consistent format, grouped into iconic houses, heritage fine jewelers, designer fine jewelry, accessible brands, and retailers.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the brand's size or the value of its jewelry.
sectionIntroductions: The most famous jewelry houses, many of them on Place Vendôme or Fifth Avenue, rely on founders' names set in timeless serifs and scripts.
Heritage fine jewelers from Italy, Japan, Britain, and Switzerland often add a founding date, an emblem, or a city to their wordmark.
Independent designers use their own names in clean, modern type that feels personal and editorial.
Accessible and demi-fine brands sell online and in malls, so their logos are bolder, simpler, and built for social media.
Jewelry retailers need logos that read from across a shopping mall or on a phone screen, so they favour bold type and strong colour.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of jewelry logos, not a ranking of jewelers.
Look at how each logo uses type, a symbol, or one detail to signal its price point and personality.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a ring box, a clasp, and a store front.

findings.heading: Jewelry logos are mostly names
findings.text: Cartier, Tiffany & Co., Harry Winston, Graff, and David Yurman all use the founder's name as the logo, so the typeface does the work.

findings.heading: Heritage is written into the logo
findings.text: Boucheron, Buccellati, Damiani, Garrard, and Helzberg add a founding year or city to their wordmark to prove their history.

findings.heading: Luxury uses serifs and scripts, mass market uses bold sans
findings.text: High jewelry favours fine serifs and calligraphy, while Pandora, Mejuri, Kay, and Tous use heavy, simple letters that read at a glance.

findings.heading: Colour lives in the packaging
findings.text: Most jewelry logos are black, while the brand colour appears on boxes and bags, like Tiffany Blue, the Cartier red, and Asprey purple.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a jewelry logo
checklistItems: Does the logo work at tiny sizes, like on a clasp, tag, or engraving?
Does the typeface match your price point, from high jewelry to demi-fine?
Could one detail, like a monogram or a custom letter, make it more memorable?
Will it look right embossed in gold foil on a ring box and a shopping bag?
Is it simple enough to engrave, stamp, or print in one colour?

faq.question: What makes a good jewelry logo?
faq.answer: A good jewelry logo is simple, refined, and readable at very small sizes. It uses carefully chosen type, often a serif or a script, and sometimes one memorable detail, like the Roman V in Bulgari or the crown on the Pandora O.

faq.question: What are the most famous jewelry brand logos?
faq.answer: The most famous jewelry logos include Cartier, Tiffany & Co., Bulgari, Van Cleef & Arpels, Harry Winston, Graff, Chopard, Pandora, and Swarovski. Most of them are wordmarks based on the founder's name.

faq.question: What fonts do luxury jewelry brands use?
faq.answer: Luxury jewelry brands use classic serif capitals, like Tiffany & Co., Bulgari, and Graff, or calligraphic scripts, like Cartier and Chopard. Accessible brands, like Pandora and Mejuri, use bold sans serifs. Most of these logos are custom-drawn.

faq.question: What colours are best for a jewelry logo?
faq.answer: Black, gold, and one signature colour work best for jewelry logos. Many brands keep the logo black and put their colour on the packaging, like Tiffany Blue, the red Cartier box, and Asprey purple.

faq.question: Should a jewelry logo have a symbol?
faq.answer: A symbol or monogram helps when the logo needs to appear on clasps, charms, and engraving. Brands like Tanishq, Buccellati, and Chaumet pair a wordmark with an emblem, while many luxury houses rely on the wordmark alone.
